migrationNotes: Spine: Maya's one remark about eating early is taken apart further on each screen: first into a claim and its reasons, then labelled by indicator words, written in standard form, completed with the premise she left out, and finally stretched into a chain where one conclusion feeds the next.

lesson.title: Finding the argument

steps.headline: A claim and the reasons given for it

lead.text: Look again at what Maya said. Her remark makes three separate claims, and they don't all do the same job. “We should eat early” is what she wants her friends to accept. “The film starts at seven” and “the restaurant is a half-hour walk away” are her reasons: facts she offers so that eating early looks like the sensible plan.

Philosophers have names for these two jobs. The claim someone wants you to accept is the conclusion. Each claim offered as a reason for it is a premise. A conclusion together with the premises offered for it is an argument. In everyday speech the word often means a quarrel, but here it means a piece of reasoning, and Maya's is a small one with two premises and one conclusion.

afterFigure.text: The figure sets her remark out as a map, with the premises above and the conclusion below. Her second sentence joins two claims with “and”, and each is a premise in its own right, so that one sentence counts as two.

Premise and conclusion are jobs that a claim does inside one piece of reasoning. “The film starts at seven” is a premise for Maya, but in a talk about cinema listings it could be somebody's conclusion. The sentence alone doesn't tell you which job it has. You have to look at what it is doing in the passage, and the next screens give you ways to do that.

model.passage: We should eat early. The film starts at seven, and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away.

premises.text: The film starts at seven.
The restaurant is a half-hour walk away.

model.passage: There will be no tables left: the queue already runs out of the door.

premises.text: The queue already runs out of the door.

conclusion.text: There will be no tables left.

lead.text: Reasons can come in a different order from Maya's. This passage gives its reasons first and its claim last. Count the claims it offers as reasons, remembering that one sentence can hold more than one.

steps.headline: Words that point to a reason or a conclusion

lead.text: Maya gave no signposts, and her friends followed her anyway. Often a speaker does add one. Words such as “because”, “since”, “for” and “after all” point to a reason, so what follows them is a premise. Words such as “so”, “hence” and “thus” point to a conclusion. They are called indicator words, and they are the quickest clue you have.

They also show that the conclusion has no fixed place. A groundsman might say that the match will be called off because the pitch is flooded, or that the pitch is flooded, so the match will be called off. The words and the order change while the two claims and their jobs stay the same. In the figure, choose Passage and press Highlight indicator words to see the signposts in each version.

afterFigure.text: Because position can't settle which claim is the conclusion, and indicator words are sometimes missing or used loosely, it helps to have a second test. Ask what the passage is trying to get you to accept. That claim is the conclusion, and the others are there to back it up. Two short passages come next, so you can try both tests.

model.passage: The match will be called off, because the pitch is flooded.

premises.text: The pitch is flooded.

conclusion.text: The match will be called off.

model.passage: Since the pitch is flooded, the match will be called off.

premises.text: The pitch is flooded.

conclusion.text: The match will be called off.

model.passage: The pitch is flooded, so the match will be called off.

premises.text: The pitch is flooded.

conclusion.text: The match will be called off.

lead.text: Indicator words are small and easy to read past. Look at the sentence below and find the one word that does the pointing.
Use the signpost, and ask what the passage as a whole is trying to get you to accept. Then give the conclusion in your own words.

steps.headline: Writing an argument out line by line

lead.text: Spoken arguments are rarely tidy. A speaker may state the conclusion first, pack two premises into one sentence and add a signpost or two. Before you judge such an argument you want to see it plainly, and there is a conventional way to do that.

Take a remark from a village-hall meeting: “We shouldn't repaint the hall yet. After all, the roof still leaks and new paint would be spoiled.” Drop the signposts, give each premise its own numbered line, draw a line under them and write the conclusion last, marked C. The figure shows the result for the hall and for a second passage, with each spoken clause matched to its line. Use the buttons to switch between them.

afterFigure.text: This layout is called standard form. It leaves the speaker's meaning alone and puts the support in view, so you can ask two separate things: whether each premise is true, and whether the premises, if true, would back the conclusion. A tangled sentence makes it hard to ask either.

It also gives you something to point at. If you disagree about the hall, you can now name the line you reject: the roof may have been mended, or perhaps new paint would survive a few drips. The next question returns to how the conclusion was picked out.

model.passage: We shouldn't repaint the hall yet. After all, the roof still leaks and new paint would be spoiled.

premises.text: The roof still leaks.
New paint would be spoiled.

conclusion.text: We shouldn't repaint the hall yet.

model.passage: You will be late for the meeting: the 8:10 has been cancelled, and the next train arrives after it starts.

premises.text: The 8:10 train has been cancelled.
The next train arrives after the meeting starts.

conclusion.text: You will be late for the meeting.

lead.text: Standard form moved the hall's conclusion to the end of the list. Think about what picked it out in the first place.

steps.headline: The reason nobody said out loud

lead.text: Maya's remark leaves something out. The film starts at seven and the restaurant is half an hour away, but those facts only point towards eating early if two more things hold: nobody wants to miss the start of the film, and dinner takes a good while. She never said either. She didn't need to, because everyone at the table already took them for granted.

Almost every real argument works this way. People leave out whatever seems too obvious to say, and the argument is shorter and smoother for it. A premise that is needed but not stated is an unstated premise, and an argument with one is called an enthymeme. The name goes back to Aristotle's Rhetoric, where it covers this kind of everyday reasoning.

afterFigure.text: To find a missing premise, ask what else would have to be true for the stated reasons to lead to the conclusion. Add it to the list and the argument is complete, so you can see what it rests on. That is often where its weak spot is. Dev's phone could be off because the battery died, and then the added premise is false and the conclusion loses its support. The next question gives you a case to try.

model.passage: We should eat early. The film starts at seven, and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away.

premises.text: The film starts at seven.
The restaurant is a half-hour walk away.
We want to be in our seats by seven.
Dinner takes a good while.

model.passage: Dev's phone is switched off, so he must be asleep.

premises.text: Dev's phone is switched off.
Dev only switches his phone off when he is asleep.

lead.text: A short argument can lean on a premise nobody says. Ask what link is missing between the reason given and the conclusion, then choose the claim that supplies it.

reveal.text: The unstated premise is the bridge, and supplying it shows where the argument is weak. Many solicitors qualified after a degree in another subject, so the premise is less safe than it looks.

model.passage: Mira is a solicitor, so she has a law degree.

premises.text: Every solicitor has a law degree.
Mira is a solicitor.

model.passage: The kettle is switched on at the wall, yet the water is cold after five minutes. So the kettle is broken.

premises.text: If the kettle is switched on at the wall and works, it heats the water.
The kettle is switched on at the wall.
The water is cold after five minutes.

steps.headline: When one conclusion feeds the next

lead.text: Real reasoning is rarely one step long. Suppose Tom asks Maya how early she means. She could answer: “The film starts at seven and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away, so we must leave the restaurant by half past six. A meal takes about an hour, so we should be sitting down by half past five.”

That is two arguments joined together. The first uses two premises to reach “we must leave the restaurant by half past six”. That claim is a conclusion, but it then serves as a premise in the second step, which adds “a meal takes about an hour” and reaches “we should be sitting down by half past five”. A conclusion that is used again as a premise is an intermediate conclusion. The claim the whole chain is aiming at is the final conclusion. The figure draws the two steps as one chain, and its buttons challenge one claim at a time.

afterFigure.text: Mapping a chain shows where an objection would do the most damage. If Tom shows that the meal takes forty minutes, only the second step is affected. If he shows that the walk takes an hour, the first conclusion changes and the second changes with it. Indicator words help here too: each “so” marks a conclusion, and the last one marks the final conclusion.

model.passage: The film starts at seven and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away, so we must leave the restaurant by half past six.

premises.text: The film starts at seven.
The restaurant is a half-hour walk away.

conclusion.text: We must leave the restaurant by half past six.

model.passage: We must leave by half past six. A meal takes about an hour, so we should be sitting down by half past five.

premises.text: We must leave the restaurant by half past six.
A meal takes about an hour.

conclusion.text: We should be sitting down by half past five.

lead.text: Now a chain from a different setting, with its own signposts. Follow the steps one at a time before you count.

lesson.orientation: Separate premises from conclusion, write an argument in standard form and supply a missing premise.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Maya and three friends are planning a Friday evening: dinner first, then a film. She glances at the clock and says, “We should eat early. The film starts at seven, and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away.” The others nod and start looking for their coats.

Suppose one of them, Tom, isn't convinced. Saying “no” will get him nowhere, because Maya has given him something to work with. To answer her properly he has to see what she is asking everyone to accept and what she is relying on to get them there. She never labelled either, and she took a few things for granted that she didn't say at all.

People reason like this at work and at home, and most of it goes by without anyone looking closely. Philosophy starts by slowing it down. The first skill in this course is taking a short piece of reasoning like Maya's apart and seeing what each claim is there to do.

intro.promise: By the end you'll take a piece of reasoning apart, write it out line by line and find the reason it leaves unsaid.

recap.keyIdea: An argument is a conclusion backed by premises. Find the conclusion first, then list the premises offered for it and add any premise the speaker took for granted.

blocks.text: You took Maya's remark apart into premises and a conclusion, used indicator words and the question of what a passage is trying to get you to accept to find the conclusion wherever it sits, and wrote a village-hall passage in standard form. You also supplied the premises that Maya and Mira left unsaid and followed a chain in which one conclusion becomes the next premise.

recap.nextHook: Laid out like this, an argument can be checked for how firmly its premises hold up its conclusion, and the next lesson gives you a test for that.

questions.prompt: Read this passage: “Since the bridge was built before 1950, and every bridge built before 1950 must be inspected this year, the bridge must be inspected this year.” How many premises does it state?
hints: Find the claim the passage wants you to accept; that is the conclusion.
'Since' introduces the reasons. List each separate claim it introduces.
Count the claims offered as reasons, leaving out the conclusion.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: the bridge's date of construction, and the rule that bridges of that age must be inspected this year. The final clause is the conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: Two premises support one conclusion. The “since” clause holds both reasons, and the final clause is the claim.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the conclusion. Count only the claims offered as reasons for it.
Look at the “and” in the “since” clause. It joins two separate claims, each offered as a reason.

questions.prompt: What is the conclusion of this passage? “The council should not sell the playing field. After all, it is the only open space in the ward, and selling a ward's only open space breaks the council's own planning policy.”
hints: Ask which sentence the others are offered to support.
The signpost “after all” points at the reasons, so look for the claim they back.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The council should not sell the playing field. “After all” introduces the reasons, so the opening sentence is the claim they support.

questions.onCorrect: “After all” announces reasons, so the opening sentence is the claim they support.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are reasons given for a claim. Ask which sentence they are given for.

questions.prompt: What is the traditional name for an argument that leaves one of its premises unstated?
hints: The term comes from Greek and is used of everyday arguments that skip an obvious step.
It begins with 'enthy-'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An enthymeme: an argument with a suppressed premise, such as 'Mira is a solicitor, so she has a law degree'.

questions.onCorrect: An enthymeme is an argument that leaves a premise unstated, as Maya's remark and Mira's do.

misconceptions.feedback: A syllogism has both premises stated. The name you want is for an argument that leaves one out.

questions.prompt: Read: 'Water expands when it freezes, so a full, sealed glass bottle left in the freezer will crack; and a cracked bottle leaks, so the freezer will need cleaning.' How many conclusions, intermediate and final, does it draw?
hints: Each 'so' introduces a conclusion.
A conclusion can be used again as a premise for a later step.
Count every claim that follows a 'so'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two. The bottle will crack (concluded from expansion), and the freezer will need cleaning (concluded from the crack and the leak).

questions.onCorrect: Two conclusions: the bottle will crack, and the freezer will need cleaning. The first becomes a premise for the second.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the last claim. The earlier “so” also draws a conclusion.
Check what follows each “so”. The water expanding is a reason, not something concluded.

questions.prompt: Read: 'Because all reptiles are cold-blooded and every snake is a reptile, and because cold-blooded animals bask in the morning sun, snakes bask in the morning sun.' How many premises does it state?
hints: Find the conclusion first; it comes at the end.
Each 'because' clause can contain more than one claim joined by 'and'.
Count the separate claims offered as reasons.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three premises: reptiles are cold-blooded; snakes are reptiles; cold-blooded animals bask in the morning sun. The final clause is the conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: Three premises. A single “because” clause can hold two claims, and the final clause is the conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the conclusion at the end. Count only the claims offered as reasons.
A “because” clause with “and” holds two claims, and there is a second “because” after it. Count every reason.

questions.prompt: In 'We should cancel the picnic, since the forecast says thunderstorms', which single word signals the premise?
hints: Look for the word that could be replaced by 'because'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Since' introduces the reason, the forecast; the conclusion is that we should cancel.

questions.onCorrect: “Since” introduces the reason, the forecast. The conclusion is what the reason supports.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are parts of the claims. Look for the small word that points at the reason.

questions.prompt: How many separate reasons does Maya give for eating early?
hints: Which sentence is the thing she wants us to do?
The rest of what she says is there to back it up. List those claims one at a time.
Count the claims offered as support, leaving out the one they back.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: the film starts at seven, and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away. “We should eat early” is what they support.

questions.onCorrect: Two reasons back one claim. Seeing which is which is the first move in judging any argument.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the claim Maya wants us to accept. It is what the reasons support, not one of them.
The second sentence joins two claims with “and”. Each is a separate reason.

questions.prompt: In “The shop must be shut, because the lights are off”, which part is the conclusion?
hints: Ask which claim the other part is there to support.
questions.onCorrect: The shop's being shut is the claim. The lights being off is offered as the reason for it.

misconceptions.feedback: The lights are the reason offered. A conclusion is the claim that a reason supports.
“Because” is an indicator word. It points at a reason; it is not a claim at all.

questions.prompt: In the passage “We shouldn't repaint the hall yet. After all, the roof still leaks and new paint would be spoiled.” why is “We shouldn't repaint the hall yet” the conclusion?
hints: What do the other sentences do for it?

acceptedIdeas: The other sentences are offered as reasons for it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The other sentences are offered as reasons for it.

choices.label: The other sentences are offered as reasons for it.
It comes first in the passage.

questions.onCorrect: What the other claims do for it decides the matter. Position and length have no say.

misconceptions.feedback: Conclusions can come last, as in “since …” passages. Where a sentence sits never settles it.
Length has nothing to do with it. Look at what the other claims are for.

questions.prompt: Which unstated premise makes “Mira is a solicitor, so she has a law degree” work as an argument?
hints: The missing premise must link being a solicitor to having a law degree.

acceptedIdeas: Every solicitor has a law degree.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every solicitor has a law degree.

choices.label: Every solicitor has a law degree.

questions.onCorrect: That premise bridges the gap between the reason and the conclusion. Without it the step is a leap.

misconceptions.feedback: That may be true, but it does not connect being a solicitor with having a degree.
That runs the wrong way. It starts from law graduates, but Mira is introduced as a solicitor.
